subject: english-language
title: Aitchison versus Halliday
welcome_lead: Two giants of change: Aitchison's metaphors and Halliday's functions. Compare their toolkits side by side.
meta_desc: Aitchison's metaphors and Halliday's functional theory of language change at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have set Aitchison and Halliday on the same bench — descriptive defence and functional explanation working in tandem.

concepts.def: Jean Aitchison's damp spoon, crumbling castle and infectious disease — three prescriptivist views she rejected.
Michael Halliday's Systemic Functional Linguistics treats language as a meaning-making resource with three metafunctions.
Language used to represent experience (transitivity, processes, participants).
Language used to enact social relationships (mood, modality).
Language used to organise discourse (theme, cohesion).
Halliday's view that language changes when speakers need to mean new things — driving lexical and grammatical innovation.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Aitchison's Reith Lectures rebutted three prescriptivist metaphors. Change is not decay (crumbling castle), nor contagion (infectious disease), nor laziness (damp spoon).

Her descriptivism opens space for Halliday's functional account: change happens because language must serve evolving uses.

Halliday's SFL frames every utterance as simultaneously ideational, interpersonal and textual. New technologies generate new ideational vocabulary (algorithm, hashtag) and new textual conventions (threading, replies).
Aitchison defends change; Halliday explains it. Together they form a robust A-Level toolkit — rebut the prescriptivist, then show what is functionally driving the innovation.

mcqs.q: Which of Aitchison's metaphors blames laziness for change?
options: Damp spoon
Crumbling castle
Infectious disease
Wave model

mcqs.q: Is language change a sign of decline?
options: No — modern linguistics treats change as natural and continuous, not as decay. Every language has always been changing and will continue to.
Language change shows that standards are falling and English is being ruined.
Spoken language has no rules unlike written language.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.

mcqs.q: What is Vygotsky's view of language development?
options: Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
Vygotsky believed children develop language alone through internal processes.
Vygotsky was a behaviourist who emphasised reinforcement.
Language develops through social interaction with more knowledgeable others — they 'scaffold' the child within the Zone of Proximal Development.

mcqs.q: Are features of spoken language like 'um' and 'you know' signs of poor speech?
options: Spoken language has no rules unlike written language.
Fillers and false starts show the speaker is uneducated.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
No — they are functional discourse markers and planning devices that help interaction flow, manage turn-taking and signal speaker meaning.
